claim: The study sample includes 197 individuals with cognitive data and 146 with cognitive and MRI data.
source: The study sample includes 197 individuals with cognitive data and 146 with cognitive and MRI data, after excluding 10 participants due to high head movement in MRI, 6 due to anatomical incompatibility with Freesurfer surface rendering, and 1 due to outlier network segregation values.
evidence: Direct statement of sample size with specific exclusion criteria documented in the manuscript.

source: The study sample includes 197 individuals with cognitive data and 146 with cognitive and MRI data, after excluding 10 participants due to high head movement in MRI, 6 due to anatomical incompatibility with Freesurfer surface rendering, and 1 due to outlier network segregation values.

claim: Participants were community-dwelling, cognitively unimpaired older adults, 85–99 years of age.
source: Participants were community-dwelling, cognitively unimpaired older adults, 85–99 years of age.
evidence: Direct statement of participant characteristics in the methods section.

claim: The segregation of the association system has strong associations with overall cognition.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: The segregation of the association system has strong associations with processing speed.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: The segregation of the fronto-parietal network has strong associations with overall cognition.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: The segregation of the default mode network has strong associations with overall cognition.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: The segregation of the fronto-parietal network has strong associations with processing speed.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: The segregation of the cingulo-opercular network has strong associations with processing speed.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: The segregation of the default mode network has strong associations with processing speed.
source: We found that the segregation of the association system and the individual networks within the association system (the fronto-parietal network , cingulo-opercular network, and default mode network), has strong associations with overall cognition and processing speed.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main findings.

claim: Network segregation of the oldest-old brain is closely linked to cognitive performance.
source: This study shows that network segregation of the oldest-old brain is closely linked to cognitive performance.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main conclusion.

claim: Cognitive ability is associated with differentiated functional networks in very old individuals representing successful cognitive aging.
source: This work adds to the growing body of knowledge about differentiation in the aged brain by demonstrating that cognitive ability is associated with differentiated functional networks in very old individuals representing successful cognitive aging.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract summarizing the main conclusion.

claim: Prior work has mostly been done in younger-old samples (largely 65–85 years old).
source: Prior work has mostly been done in younger-old samples (largely 65–85 years old).
evidence: Statement about the existing literature in the introduction.

claim: Studies of the younger-old can be confounded by inclusion of pre-symptomatic disease.
source: Studies of the younger-old can be confounded by inclusion of pre-symptomatic disease since it is unknown which individuals may be experiencing undetectable, preclinical cognitive disorders and which will continue to be cognitively healthy for another decade.
evidence: Reasoning about limitations of prior research presented in the introduction.

claim: There is greater variability in both performance on neurocognitive tasks and brain connectivity measures in oldest-old compared to younger cohorts.
source: This increased variance makes it easier to observe across-subject relationships of cognition and brain networks (Gratton et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Intact cognition in the healthy oldest-old is impacted by cognitive reserve.
source: Prior work studying the healthy oldest-old indicates intact cognition in this age group is impacted by influences such as cognitive reserve (Kawas et al., 2021) and resistance to Alzheimer's disease-related neuropathology (Biswas et al., 2023; Gefen et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Intact cognition in the healthy oldest-old is impacted by resistance to Alzheimer's disease-related neuropathology.
source: Prior work studying the healthy oldest-old indicates intact cognition in this age group is impacted by influences such as cognitive reserve (Kawas et al., 2021) and resistance to Alzheimer's disease-related neuropathology (Biswas et al., 2023; Gefen et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Processing speed refers to the speed with which cognitive processes, such as reasoning and memory, can be executed.
source: Processing speed refers to the speed with which cognitive processes, such as reasoning and memory, can be executed (Sliwinski and Buschke, 1997).
evidence: Definition supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cognitive aging is associated with impairment in processing speed, which in turn may lead to a cascade of age-associated deficits in other cognitive abilities.
source: Salthouse, 1996 proposed that cognitive aging is associated with impairment in processing speed, which in turn may lead to a cascade of age-associated deficits in other cognitive abilities.
evidence: Statement about a theoretical proposal supported by citation.

claim: Executive functioning performance reliably declines in normal aging.
source: Executive functioning performance reliably declines in normal aging (Fisk and Sharp, 2004; Harada et al., 2013; Reuter-Lorenz, 2016; Salthouse et al., 2003; Spaan, 2015), and this decline is faster in older ages (Zaninotto et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Executive functioning decline is faster in older ages.
source: Executive functioning performance reliably declines in normal aging (Fisk and Sharp, 2004; Harada et al., 2013; Reuter-Lorenz, 2016; Salthouse et al., 2003; Spaan, 2015), and this decline is faster in older ages (Zaninotto et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Age-related decline in memory is reported subjectively by most older adults.
source: Age-related decline in memory is reported subjectively by most older adults (Craik, 2008), with episodic memory being the most impacted by aging compared to other memory systems (Luo and Craik, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Episodic memory is the most impacted by aging compared to other memory systems.
source: Age-related decline in memory is reported subjectively by most older adults (Craik, 2008), with episodic memory being the most impacted by aging compared to other memory systems (Luo and Craik, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Working memory gradually declines from early to late adulthood.
source: There is reliable evidence across studies that working memory gradually declines from early to late adulthood (Kidder et al., 1997; Salthouse and Babcock, 1991; Stanley et al., 2015; Vaqué-Alcázar et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Language production undergoes age-related decline.
source: Language function, particularly language production, also undergoes age-related decline and is related to other cognitive functions affected by aging, including working memory and executive function (Rizio and Diaz, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Language production is related to working memory and executive function.
source: Language function, particularly language production, also undergoes age-related decline and is related to other cognitive functions affected by aging, including working memory and executive function (Rizio and Diaz, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Older adults exhibit differences in brain structural and functional network integrity that impact network dynamics.
source: Brain networks play a crucial role in aging, and older adults exhibit differences in brain structural and functional network integrity that impact network dynamics (Marstaller et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In older adults, functional networks have increased between-network connectivity and decreased within-network connectivity, which in turn decreases segregation.
source: In older adults, functional networks have increased between-network connectivity and decreased within-network connectivity, which in turn decreases segregation (Chan et al., 2017; Damoiseaux, 2017; Iordan et al., 2017; Koen et al., 2020; Varangis et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The dedifferentiation hypothesis posits that as we age, brain networks lose their specialized functions, becoming less selectively organized and more homogenous in their activity.
source: This hypothesis posits that as we age, brain networks lose their specialized functions, becoming less selectively organized and more homogenous in their activity (McDonough et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about a theoretical hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Dedifferentiation of higher-order cognitive networks of the association system are related to poorer performance in many cognitive abilities, including episodic memory, processing speed, attention, and executive function.
source: Previous studies have found that dedifferentiation of higher-order cognitive networks of the association system —the fronto-parietal network (FPN), cingulo-opercular network (CON), and default mode network (DMN)—are related to poorer performance in many cognitive abilities, including episodic memory, processing speed, attention, and executive function (Chan et al., 2017; Damoiseaux, 2017; Goh, 2011; Hausman et al., 2020; Iordan et al., 2017; Koen et al., 2020; Nashiro et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2016; Varangis et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The FPN is associated with complex attention and directing cognitive control.
source: The FPN is associated with complex attention and directing cognitive control (Avelar-Pereira et al., 2017; Malagurski et al., 2020; Oschmann and Gawryluk, 2020; Ray et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The CON is associated with sustained executive control and perceptual and attentional task maintenance.
source: The CON is associated with sustained executive control and perceptual and attentional task maintenance (Coste and Kleinschmidt, 2016; Hausman et al., 2020; Sadaghiani and D'Esposito, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The DMN is activated during rest, internally focused tasks, and memory processing.
source: The DMN is activated during rest, internally focused tasks, and memory processing, but is suppressed during cognitively demanding, externally focused tasks (Avelar-Pereira et al., 2017; Hampson et al., 2006; Hellyer et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2016; Sambataro et al., 2010; Sestieri et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The DMN is suppressed during cognitively demanding, externally focused tasks.
source: The DMN is activated during rest, internally focused tasks, and memory processing, but is suppressed during cognitively demanding, externally focused tasks (Avelar-Pereira et al., 2017; Hampson et al., 2006; Hellyer et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2016; Sambataro et al., 2010; Sestieri et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Processing speed has been shown to be related to the FPN, CON, and DMN.
source: Processing speed has been shown to be related to all of these networks (Ruiz-Rizzo et al., 2019; Sheffield et al., 2015; Staffaroni et al., 2018; Vatansever et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: With a sample size of 146, an alpha of 0.05, and a power of 0.80, all analyses can detect small effect sizes, with the smallest detectable effect for a correlation being r = 0.23.
source: A power analysis was performed which indicated that with a sample size of 146, an alpha of 0.05, and a power of 0.80, all analyses can detect small effect sizes, with the smallest detectable effect for a correlation being r = 0.23.
evidence: Direct statement of power analysis results.

claim: This study is sufficiently powered to detect results similar to the effect size found by Chan et al., 2014.
source: This result indicated this study is sufficiently powered to detect results similar to the effect size found by Chan et al., 2014.
evidence: Statement about power analysis in relation to prior work.

claim: Exploratory factor analysis revealed five cognitive factors: processing speed, episodic memory, executive functioning, working memory, and language.
source: Exploratory factor analysis (section 'Cognitive measures') revealed five cognitive factors: (1) processing speed, (2) episodic memory, (3) executive functioning, (4) working memory, and (5) language (see Supplementary file 1 for variable factor loadings).
evidence: Direct statement of factor analysis results.

claim: Overall cognition was calculated as the average of an individual's factor scores across the five factors.
source: Overall cognition was calculated as the average of an individual's factor scores across the five factors.
evidence: Direct statement of how overall cognition was calculated.

claim: The sample had a mean association system segregation of 0.4205.
source: Our sample had a mean association system segregation of 0.4205, which is consistent with previous older adult cohorts from Chan et al., 2014 (n = 60, 65–89 years) mean association system segregation of 0.40 (Chan et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and Han et al., 2018 (n = 46, 80–93 years) mean association system segregation of <0.50 (Han et al., 2018; Figure 7).
evidence: Direct statement of descriptive statistics.

claim: The mean association system segregation of 0.4205 is consistent with previous older adult cohorts from Chan et al., 2014 (n = 60, 65–89 years) mean association system segregation of 0.40.
source: Our sample had a mean association system segregation of 0.4205, which is consistent with previous older adult cohorts from Chan et al., 2014 (n = 60, 65–89 years) mean association system segregation of 0.40 (Chan et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and Han et al., 2018 (n = 46, 80–93 years) mean association system segregation of <0.50 (Han et al., 2018; Figure 7).
evidence: Comparison of current data to prior work supported by citation.

claim: The mean association system segregation of 0.4205 is consistent with Han et al., 2018 (n = 46, 80–93 years) mean association system segregation of <0.50.
source: Our sample had a mean association system segregation of 0.4205, which is consistent with previous older adult cohorts from Chan et al., 2014 (n = 60, 65–89 years) mean association system segregation of 0.40 (Chan et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and Han et al., 2018 (n = 46, 80–93 years) mean association system segregation of <0.50 (Han et al., 2018; Figure 7).
evidence: Comparison of current data to prior work supported by citation.

claim: Overall cognition was related to association system segregation (r = 0.233, p=0.004).
source: Overall cognition was related to association system segregation (r = 0.233, p=0.004), modularity (r = 0.232, p=0.005), and mean within-network connectivity (r = 0.164, p=0.048), but not participation coefficient (r = –0.112, p=0.178) (Figure 3, section 'Relating cognition to network metrics').
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results with reference to figure.

claim: Overall cognition was related to association system modularity (r = 0.232, p=0.005).
source: Overall cognition was related to association system segregation (r = 0.233, p=0.004), modularity (r = 0.232, p=0.005), and mean within-network connectivity (r = 0.164, p=0.048), but not participation coefficient (r = –0.112, p=0.178) (Figure 3, section 'Relating cognition to network metrics').
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results with reference to figure.

claim: Overall cognition was related to association system mean within-network connectivity (r = 0.164, p=0.048).
source: Overall cognition was related to association system segregation (r = 0.233, p=0.004), modularity (r = 0.232, p=0.005), and mean within-network connectivity (r = 0.164, p=0.048), but not participation coefficient (r = –0.112, p=0.178) (Figure 3, section 'Relating cognition to network metrics').
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results with reference to figure.

claim: Overall cognition was not related to association system participation coefficient (r = –0.112, p=0.178).
source: Overall cognition was related to association system segregation (r = 0.233, p=0.004), modularity (r = 0.232, p=0.005), and mean within-network connectivity (r = 0.164, p=0.048), but not participation coefficient (r = –0.112, p=0.178) (Figure 3, section 'Relating cognition to network metrics').
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results with reference to figure.

claim: Only segregation and modularity remained significant after multiple comparisons correction using false discovery rate (FDR).
source: Only segregation and modularity remained significant after multiple comparisons correction using false discovery rate (FDR) (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: Direct statement of results after multiple comparison correction.

claim: There was a strong, significant relationship between association system segregation and modularity (r = 0.573, p<0.001).
source: There was a strong, significant relationship between association system segregation and modularity (r = 0.573, p<0.001).
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results.

claim: Processing speed was related to all networks' segregation (FPN, CON, and DMN).
source: Processing speed was related to all networks' segregation (Figure 5).
evidence: Direct statement of results with reference to figure.

claim: The relationships between processing speed and network segregation were still significant after correction for multiple comparisons using FDR.
source: These relationships were still significant after correction for multiple comparisons using FDR, partial correlation with site as a covariate, and partial correlation with cortical thickness as a covariate.
evidence: Direct statement of results after multiple comparison correction and covariate analysis.

claim: The relationships between processing speed and network segregation were still significant after partial correlation with site as a covariate.
source: These relationships were still significant after correction for multiple comparisons using FDR, partial correlation with site as a covariate, and partial correlation with cortical thickness as a covariate.
evidence: Direct statement of results after covariate analysis.

claim: The relationships between processing speed and network segregation were still significant after partial correlation with cortical thickness as a covariate.
source: These relationships were still significant after correction for multiple comparisons using FDR, partial correlation with site as a covariate, and partial correlation with cortical thickness as a covariate.
evidence: Direct statement of results after covariate analysis.

claim: The correlations between processing speed and network segregation were evident when using alternative parcellations indicating replicability of these results.
source: Additionally, these correlations were evident when using the alternative parcellations indicating replicability of these results (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Direct statement of replication analysis with reference to figure.

claim: Executive functioning was only significantly related to FPN segregation.
source: Executive functioning was only significantly related to FPN segregation.
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results.

claim: The relationship between executive functioning and FPN segregation was no longer significant after multiple comparison corrections.
source: However, this relationship was no longer significant after multiple comparison corrections.
evidence: Direct statement of results after multiple comparison correction.

claim: Correlations between executive functioning, memory, working memory, and language and the FPN, DMN, and CON segregation were very weak and not significant.
source: Correlations between executive functioning, memory, working memory, and language and the FPN, DMN, and CON segregation were very weak and not significant (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results.

claim: Association system segregation was not correlated with memory (r = –0.02, p=0.805).
source: To compare with prior findings, we analyzed the relationship between association system segregation and memory, which was not correlated as had been previously found in the work by Chan et al., 2017 (r = –0.02, p=0.805).
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results comparing to prior work.

claim: Network nodes were created based on methods developed by Chan et al., 2014 and Han et al., 2018 for the oldest-old sample.
source: We created network nodes based on methods developed by Chan et al., 2014 and Han et al., 2018 for our oldest-old sample (Figure 1, section 'Network nodes').
evidence: Direct statement of methods with reference to prior work and figure.

claim: The association system consists of the default mode network (DMN), fronto-parietal control network (FPN), ventral attention network (VA), cingulo-opercular control network (CON), and dorsal attention network (DA).
source: The association system consists of the default mode (DMN; red), fronto-parietal control (FPN; yellow), ventral attention (VA; teal), cingulo-opercular control (CON; purple), and dorsal attention (DA; green).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The sensory-motor system consists of the hand somato-motor, visual, mouth somato-motor, and auditory networks.
source: The sensory-motor system consists of the hand somato-motor (light blue), visual (blue), mouth somato-motor (M; orange), and auditory networks (Aud; pink).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Data were collected from four McKnight Institutes: the University of Alabama at Birmingham, the University of Florida, the University of Miami, and the University of Arizona.
source: Data were collected from the four McKnight Institutes: the University of Alabama at Birmingham, the University of Florida, the University of Miami, and the University of Arizona.
evidence: Direct statement of data collection sites.

claim: An 8-minute resting-state functional scan was collected for all subjects.
source: After the anatomical scan, an 8-minute resting-state functional scan was collected (T2*-weighted, TE/TR 30/2400 ms; FOV = 140 × 5 × 140; FA = 70°; voxel size = 3.0 × 3.0 × 3.0 mm; interleaved order of acquisition).
evidence: Direct statement of imaging acquisition parameters.

claim: Participants were instructed to stay awake, keep their eyes open, and let their minds wander without thinking of anything in particular during the resting-state scan.
source: Before the functional scan, participants were instructed to try to be as still as possible, stay awake, keep their eyes open, and let their minds wander without thinking of anything in particular.
evidence: Direct statement of participant instructions.

claim: Anatomical images were preprocessed through Freesurfer (version 6.0) to render cortical surfaces.
source: Anatomical images were preprocessed through Freesurfer (version 6.0) to render cortical surfaces (Fischl, 2012).
evidence: Direct statement of preprocessing methods with citation.

claim: Functional data were preprocessed with XCPEngine and fMRIPrep.
source: Before functional connectivity analysis, data were preprocessed with rigorous quality control methods for motion censoring (Carp, 2013; Gratton et al., 2020; Power et al., 2012; Power et al., 2015; Siegel et al., 2014), implemented by XCPEngine (Ciric et al., 2018) and fMRIPrep (Esteban et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement of preprocessing methods with citations.

claim: Censoring included a framewise displacement threshold of 0.5 mm.
source: Censoring included a framewise displacement threshold of 0.5 mm, a DVARS (derivative of the root mean square) threshold of 5, a high-pass filter of 0.01, and a low-pass filter of 0.08.
evidence: Direct statement of preprocessing parameters.

claim: Spatial smoothing of 6 mm full-width-half-max was applied.
source: Spatial smoothing of 6 mm full-width-half-max was applied.
evidence: Direct statement of preprocessing parameters.

claim: Segregation was calculated as within-network connectivity minus between-network connectivity, divided by within-network connectivity.
source: Segregation was calculated as within-network connectivity minus between-network connectivity, divided by within-network connectivity (Chan et al., 2014; Wig, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement of calculation method with citations.

claim: Participation coefficient and modularity were calculated using the Brain Connectivity Toolbox.
source: Participation coefficient and modularity were calculated using the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (Rubinov and Sporns, 2010).
evidence: Direct statement of calculation method with citation.

claim: Cortical thickness was used as a covariate because in elderly populations, there is more likelihood of age-related brain changes such as atrophy.
source: Cortical thickness was used as a covariate because in elderly populations, there is more likelihood of age-related brain changes such as atrophy.
evidence: Direct statement of rationale for covariate selection.

claim: Site of data collection was included as a covariate in analyses.
source: Since data were collected across multiple sites, site-related differences in data collection could occur. Though we took substantial measures to mitigate this potential bias (testing administration training and quality control, MRI sequence homogenization, and frequent assessments of drift throughout data collection), we included site of data collection as a covariate in analyses.
evidence: Direct statement of covariate inclusion and rationale.

claim: The relationship between age and cortical thickness was not significant (r = –0.05, p=0.543).
source: The small effect and insignificant result (r = –0.05, p=0.543) is consistent with the restricted age range (span of 14 years) and with the intentionally homogenous cognitive status of the sample.
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The insignificant relationship between age and cortical thickness is consistent with the restricted age range (span of 14 years).
source: The small effect and insignificant result (r = –0.05, p=0.543) is consistent with the restricted age range (span of 14 years) and with the intentionally homogenous cognitive status of the sample.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation of results.

claim: The insignificant relationship between age and cortical thickness is consistent with the intentionally homogenous cognitive status of the sample.
source: The small effect and insignificant result (r = –0.05, p=0.543) is consistent with the restricted age range (span of 14 years) and with the intentionally homogenous cognitive status of the sample.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation of results.

claim: The study provides a healthy oldest-old (85+) cortical parcellation that can be used in future work in this age group.
source: We also provide a healthy oldest-old (85+) cortical parcellation that can be used in future work in this age group.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about a contribution of the study.

claim: Better cognitive aging seems to be related to a narrow range of relatively high neural network segregation.
source: Better cognitive aging seems to be related to a narrow range of relatively high neural network segregation.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation in the discussion.

claim: The effect of network segregation on cognition is specific to the relationship of processing speed to elements of the association networks.
source: This effect is specific to the relationship of processing speed to elements of the association networks.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation in the discussion.

claim: The FPN regulates other brain networks to support cognitive functioning.
source: Recent research indicates that the FPN regulates other brain networks to support cognitive functioning (Avelar-Pereira et al., 2017; Marstaller et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The FPN and DMN interact less efficiently in older adults compared to younger adults.
source: The FPN and DMN interact less efficiently in older adults compared to younger adults; the networks are coupled during rest and across tasks in older adults, suggesting that aging causes the FPN to have more difficulty flexibly engaging and disengaging networks (Avelar-Pereira et al., 2017; Grady et al., 2016; Spreng and Schacter, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Age-related within-network structural changes and between-network functional dedifferentiation may disrupt the FPN's ability to control other networks, like the DMN and CON.
source: Age-related within-network structural changes and between-network functional dedifferentiation may disrupt the FPN's ability to control other networks, like the DMN and CON (Avelar-Pereira et al., 2017; Geerligs et al., 2015; Grady et al., 2016; Marstaller et al., 2015; Romero-Garcia et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Age-related disruptions in FPN connectivity may explain the initial and most noticeable difference in cognition, processing speed.
source: Because of the FPN's function as a control network, age-related disruptions in FPN connectivity may explain the initial and most noticeable difference in cognition, processing speed (Ng et al., 2016; Oschmann and Gawryluk, 2020; Rieck et al., 2021a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Processing speed might be linked to the maintained segregation of key brain networks, specifically the DMN, the CON, and the FPN.
source: Our results suggest that processing speed might be linked to the maintained segregation of key brain networks, specifically the DMN, the CON, and the FPN.
evidence: Statement of interpretation of results in the discussion.

claim: Effective cognitive functioning in the oldest-old could be associated with the continued distinctiveness and specialization of the DMN, CON, and FPN.
source: This implies that despite the overall trend toward dedifferentiation that occurs in aging, effective cognitive functioning in the oldest-old could be associated with the continued distinctiveness and specialization of these critical networks.
evidence: Statement of interpretation of results in the discussion.

claim: Segregation may serve as a more sensitive metric than other network metrics when assessing cognition in aging populations.
source: With segregation's connection to cognition, it may serve as a more sensitive metric than other network metrics when assessing cognition in aging populations.
evidence: Statement of interpretation of results in the discussion.

claim: Segregation may be a marker of potential cognitive resilience in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Additionally, our work helps inform other research that has indicated that segregation may be a marker of potential cognitive resilience in Alzheimer's disease (Ewers et al., 2021) and prior work has begun to investigate its usage as a marker for future cognitive status (Chan et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Learning-induced plasticity through cognitive training and exercise could be an avenue for changing network dynamics to improve cognitive performance.
source: Studies have shown that learning-induced plasticity through cognitive training and exercise could be an avenue for changing network dynamics to improve cognitive performance (Iordan et al., 2017; Voss et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The generalizability of the findings is limited due to the limited diversity of the sample which is mostly non-Hispanic, Caucasian, and highly educated individuals.
source: We also recognize that the generalizability of our findings is limited due to the limited diversity of our sample which is mostly non-Hispanic, Caucasian, and highly educated individuals.
evidence: Direct statement of study limitation in the discussion.

claim: Factors such as race, ethnicity, and education can influence association system segregation.
source: Prior work has shown that these factors can influence association system segregation (Chan et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cross-sectional nature of the work limits information about participants' state of health and cognitive performance earlier in life or what their cognitive health will be later in life.
source: Given the cross-sectional nature of this work, we have limited information about our participants' state of health and cognitive performance earlier in life or what their cognitive health will be later in life.
evidence: Direct statement of study limitation in the discussion.

claim: Brain network organization can change across the lifespan.

claim: Functional connectivity boundary-based parcellation of the human cortex is generally consistent across the lifespan.
source: Han et al., 2018 showed that while functional connectivity boundary-based parcellation of the human cortex was generally consistent across the lifespan, the boundaries become less similar to the younger adult boundaries as cohorts get older.
